t: Pairing Cigars with Spirits: A Guide to 16 Popular Spirits
s: Over the years, the most common question we've been asked is some version of "What cigar should I smoke with this?" So we've put together a guide to 16 of the most…
x: Over the years, the most common question we've been asked is some version of "What cigar should I smoke with this?" So we've put together a guide to 16 of the most popular spirits and fortified wines. Each one has its own in-depth article covering where it comes from, where it's traditionally made, how it's made, and what to look for in a cigar to pair with it. Before you dive in, here's a quick refresher on how we pair . A great pair is balanced in four areas: Strength – match the cigar's body to the drink's intensity and alcohol. A mild cigar disappears next to a cask-strength whisky. A full-bodied maduro bulldozes a delicate fino sherry. Flavour – look for shared notes (vanilla, nuts, cocoa, cedar, leather) to complement each other, or opposite ones to create contrast (a sweet maduro against a smoky Scotch). Richness – balance the mouthfeel. A dry drink and a dry cigar leave you parched. A sweet, heavy drink wants an earthy or spicy cigar to cut through it. History – a cigar and drink from the same country, or with an intertwined story, make the experience more memorable. Most of all, remember the golden rule: in a truly great pair, the cigar makes the drink better and the drink makes the cigar better. Whisky Scotch – Match the cigar to the style. Choose a Cameroon or Connecticut cigar for light Speyside and Lowland malts, a maduro for sherried malts, and a full-bodied, earthy cigar (or a sweet maduro for contrast) for peated Islay. Bourbon – Medium to full cigars with cocoa, coffee and caramel. Maduros are a natural match, and peppery Nicaraguans suit high-rye bourbons. Irish Whiskey – Smooth and honeyed, so go mild to medium with creamy Connecticut or Cameroon wrappers. Canadian Whisky and Rye – Match rye's spice with a peppery Habano or Nicaraguan cigar, or soften it with a sweet maduro. Light Canadian blends want a mild cigar. Japanese Whisky – Delicate and precise. Choose refined, mild to medium cigars with cedar and cream. Brandy Cognac – Elegant, so pick a medium cigar with cedar, cream and baking spice. Avoid heavy maduros. Armagnac – Bolder and more rustic than cognac. It needs a medium-full to full cigar with earth, wood and dried fruit. Spanish Brandy – Rich and sweet from sherry casks. Pair with dark, full-bodied maduros with chocolate and leather. Calvados – Apple brandy with baking spice. Mild to medium Connecticut and Cameroon cigars work like cream on apple pie. Cane and Agave Rum – A natural partner for cigars. Aged rums love maduros with cocoa and coffee, and pairing by country of origin is a fun bonus. Tequila – Follow the age statement: mild cigars for blanco, medium for reposado, and medium-full maduros for añejo. Mezcal – Smoke meets smoke. Choose a full-bodied maduro, ideally with a Mexican San Andrés wrapper, to balance the roast. Fortified Wine Port – Rich, dark cigars for ruby and vintage port. Nutty, medium cigars for tawny. Sherry – Mild Connecticut cigars for fino, medium Cuban or Habano cigars for amontillado and oloroso, and a full maduro for sweet Pedro Ximénez. White Spirits Gin – Light cigars with cedar and cream let the juniper and citrus shine. A gin and tonic with a mild cigar is a summer classic. Vodka – Treat it as an ice-cold palate cleanser and pair it with a mild, creamy Connecticut. Keep Exploring These guides are a starting point, not a rulebook. Everyone's palate is different, and some of our favourite pairs broke the "rules" completely. Browse all of our pairing reviews , dig into our Whisky 101 and brandy guides, and most importantly, try things for yourself. And please, enjoy responsibly.

t: Scotch Whisky: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: Scotch is the drink that started most of our pairing nights, and it's still the one we reach for most often. It's also one of the most varied spirits on the planet.…
x: Scotch is the drink that started most of our pairing nights, and it's still the one we reach for most often. It's also one of the most varied spirits on the planet. A gentle Lowland malt and a peat-soaked Islay dram are both "Scotch," but they call for very different cigars. Here's a primer on where it comes from, how it's made, and how to pick a cigar that makes it sing. Origin The first written record of Scotch whisky appears in the Scottish Exchequer Rolls of 1494, which list "eight bolls of malt to Friar John Cor wherewith to make aqua vitae." Aqua vitae, "water of life," became uisge beatha in Gaelic, and eventually just "whisky." For centuries most distilling was small, rural and often illegal. The Excise Act of 1823 made licensed distilling affordable, and many of the distilleries we know today were founded in the decades that followed. Two events then turned Scotch into a global drink: Aeneas Coffey's continuous column still (patented in 1830), which made lighter grain whisky for blending, and the phylloxera plague that wiped out French vineyards in the late 1800s, leaving cognac drinkers looking for something new. Where It's Traditionally Made By law, Scotch must be distilled and matured in Scotland. The whisky regions are a useful shorthand for flavour: Speyside – the heart of malt whisky, with the most distilleries. Elegant, fruity and often sherried. Think Macallan, Glenfiddich, Aberlour and Balvenie. Highlands – a huge region with huge variety, from honeyed and floral to rich and lightly smoky. Glenmorangie, Dalmore, Oban and Dalwhinnie. Lowlands – traditionally lighter, softer and grassy, often triple distilled. Auchentoshan and Glenkinchie. Islay – the island of peat smoke, seaweed and iodine. Laphroaig, Ardbeg and Lagavulin. Campbeltown – once the whisky capital of the world, now home to just a few distilleries. Briny, oily and a little smoky. Springbank and Glen Scotia. You'll also hear about the "Islands" (Highland Park, Talisker, Jura), which are officially part of the Highland region but have a coastal, often smoky character of their own. How It's Made Single malt Scotch starts with just three ingredients: malted barley, water and yeast. The barley is soaked and allowed to germinate, then dried in a kiln. If the kiln is fired with peat, the smoke soaks into the grain. That's where Islay's medicinal smokiness comes from. The dried malt is ground, mixed with hot water to release its sugars, and fermented into a beer-like "wash" of around 8% alcohol. The wash is then distilled, usually twice, in copper pot stills. The shape of those stills has a big influence on how heavy or light the final spirit is. The new spirit goes into oak casks, most often ex-bourbon barrels or ex-sherry butts, and must age for at least three years in Scotland. The age on the label is the age of the youngest whisky in the bottle. You'll see five categories: Single Malt (one distillery, malted barley, pot stills), Single Grain, Blended Malt, Blended Grain, and Blended Scotch, which is the vast majority of what's sold. What It Tastes Like Bourbon-cask Scotch leans toward vanilla, honey, citrus and orchard fruit. Sherry casks add dried fruit, Christmas cake, cinnamon and chocolate. Peat brings smoke, iodine, tar and sea spray. Older whiskies gain depth and lose some fire. Cask-strength bottlings can run past 55% and need a cigar with the muscle to stand up to them. What to Look for in a Cigar Pairing Scotch is really about pairing the style of Scotch, so start by figuring out which family your bottle belongs to. Light and floral (Lowland, lighter Highland and Speyside): Choose a mild to medium cigar so you don't bulldoze the whisky. Connecticut shade or Cameroon wrappers with cream, cedar, nuts and a touch of sweetness work beautifully. Try an Arturo Fuente Hemingway (Cameroon wrapper, cedar and gentle spice). Sherried and rich (Macallan, Aberlour A'bunadh, Glendronach): Here you can go medium to full. Look for Habano or Maduro wrappers

t: Bourbon: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: If Scotch is the dram we contemplate, bourbon is the one we pour when friends come over. It's sweet, approachable and full of the same caramel, vanilla and toasted oak flavours you…
x: If Scotch is the dram we contemplate, bourbon is the one we pour when friends come over. It's sweet, approachable and full of the same caramel, vanilla and toasted oak flavours you find in a good cigar, which makes it one of the easiest spirits to pair. Here's what makes bourbon bourbon, and how to find its perfect smoke. Origin Bourbon was born on the American frontier in the late 1700s. Scots-Irish and German settlers moving into Kentucky, then still part of Virginia, brought distilling know-how with them. They found that corn grew far better there than the barley and rye they were used to. Whiskey was an easy way to turn a bulky grain harvest into something that kept and travelled well. The name most likely comes from Bourbon County in Kentucky, or from Bourbon Street in New Orleans, where much of the whiskey shipped down the Ohio and Mississippi rivers was sold. Popular stories credit Baptist preacher Elijah Craig with inventing the charred barrel, but there's no real evidence for it. Bourbon's rules were firmed up over time: the Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 guaranteed quality, and in 1964 Congress declared bourbon "a distinctive product of the United States." Where It's Traditionally Made Bourbon can legally be made anywhere in the United States, but Kentucky produces the overwhelming majority of it. The limestone-filtered water, hot summers and cold winters are credited with shaping its character. Bardstown, Louisville, Frankfort and Lawrenceburg are home to names like Buffalo Trace, Maker's Mark, Wild Turkey, Four Roses, Heaven Hill and Woodford Reserve. Tennessee whiskey, like Jack Daniel's, is made almost exactly the same way. Its defining extra step is the Lincoln County Process: the new spirit is filtered through sugar-maple charcoal before it goes into the barrel. How It's Made US law sets out strict rules for bourbon: The mash must contain at least 51% corn . The rest is usually rye or wheat, plus a little malted barley. It must be distilled to no more than 80% alcohol (160 proof). It must be aged in new, charred oak containers , and go into the barrel at no more than 62.5% (125 proof). It must be bottled at 40% (80 proof) or more, with nothing added except water. Most distillers use a "sour mash" process, where a portion of the previous batch goes into the new fermentation to keep things consistent. The beer is usually distilled first in a tall column still, then a second time in a "doubler" or "thumper." Because the barrels are brand new and heavily charred, bourbon picks up colour and flavour quickly. Barrels age in multi-storey rickhouses, where Kentucky's temperature swings push the spirit in and out of the wood. "Straight bourbon" must be aged at least two years, and if it's under four years old the age has to appear on the label. "Bottled-in-bond" means a single distillery, a single season, at least four years old and exactly 100 proof. What It Tastes Like Caramel, vanilla, toffee, toasted oak and baking spice are the backbone of every bourbon. The "mash bill" fine-tunes the profile: Wheated bourbons (Maker's Mark, Weller, Larceny) are soft, round and sweet. High-rye bourbons (Four Roses, Basil Hayden, Bulleit) are spicier, drier and peppery. Barrel-proof bourbons can top 60% alcohol and are intensely rich, with dark caramel, cherry and leather. What to Look for in a Cigar Bourbon and cigars share so many flavours that it's easy to make a good pair. The trick to a great pair is matching the strength and steering the sweetness. Strength: Most bourbons are medium to full, so start with a medium to full-bodied cigar. A mild Connecticut can work with a soft, wheated bourbon, but it will disappear next to barrel proof. Wrapper: Maduro wrappers bring natural sweetness, cocoa and coffee that mirror bourbon's caramel. Habano and Nicaraguan wrappers add pepper that lines up with high-rye bourbons. Connecticut and Ecuadorian shade wrappers suit lighter, wheated bottles. Flavours to look for: Cocoa, coffee, molasses,

t: Irish Whiskey: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: Irish whiskey has a reputation for being smooth, and it's well earned. Most of it is unpeated and many bottles are triple distilled, which makes it soft, honeyed and easy to sip.…
x: Irish whiskey has a reputation for being smooth, and it's well earned. Most of it is unpeated and many bottles are triple distilled, which makes it soft, honeyed and easy to sip. That gentleness is exactly why it rewards a thoughtful cigar choice. Pick the wrong stick and you'll never taste the whiskey at all. Origin Ireland has a strong claim to being the birthplace of whiskey. Legend says Irish monks brought distilling back from the Mediterranean in the early Middle Ages. The first written record comes from the Annals of Clonmacnoise in 1405, which note that a chieftain died after "taking a surfeit of aqua vitae" at Christmas. Old Bushmills in County Antrim traces its licence back to 1608. By the 19th century, Irish whiskey was the most popular whiskey in the world, and Dublin's huge distilleries dwarfed anything in Scotland. Then came a string of disasters: the Irish War of Independence, a trade war with Britain that closed off the Empire, and American Prohibition. By the 1970s only two distilleries were left in all of Ireland, Midleton and Bushmills. The comeback since then has been remarkable, and the island is now home to dozens of distilleries again. Where It's Traditionally Made Irish whiskey must be distilled and aged on the island of Ireland, in either the Republic or Northern Ireland. Big names include Jameson, Redbreast, Powers and Green Spot (all from Midleton in County Cork), Bushmills in County Antrim, and Tullamore D.E.W. in County Offaly. Newer distilleries like Teeling in Dublin and Waterford in the southeast are pushing the category in new directions. How It's Made Irish whiskey can be made from any cereal grain. It must be distilled to no more than 94.8% alcohol, aged for at least three years in wooden casks in Ireland, and bottled at 40% or more. There are four official styles: Single Malt – 100% malted barley from one distillery, usually in pot stills. Bushmills 10 and 16 are good examples. Single Pot Still – uniquely Irish. A mash of both malted and unmalted barley distilled in pot stills, which gives a creamy, oily texture and spicy kick. Redbreast and Green Spot are the classics. Single Grain – made mostly from corn or wheat in column stills. Light and sweet. Blended – a mix of two or more of the above. Jameson and Tullamore D.E.W. are blends. Triple distillation isn't required, but it's traditional at many distilleries and produces a lighter, purer spirit. Most Irish malt is dried in closed kilns rather than over peat fires, so the whiskey rarely has the smokiness of Scotch. Aging usually happens in ex-bourbon barrels, often finished in sherry, port or even stout casks. What It Tastes Like Expect honey, vanilla, green apple, pear, light cereal and a gentle spice. Single pot still whiskeys add a creamy mouthfeel with clove, ginger and dried fruit. Older and sherry-finished bottles bring toffee, nuts and Christmas cake. Overall, Irish whiskey is lighter and sweeter than most Scotch and less oaky than bourbon. What to Look for in a Cigar Irish whiskey's delicacy is the key. You want a cigar that adds to it rather than smothers it. Strength: Mild to medium for blends and lighter single malts. You can step up to medium, or even medium-full, for single pot still and older sherry-finished whiskeys. Wrapper: Connecticut shade and Cameroon wrappers are ideal. They bring cream, cedar and a light sweetness that lines up with the whiskey's honey. Save dark maduros for the richest pot still bottlings. Flavours to look for: Cream, toasted nuts, cedar, light baking spice and a hint of floral sweetness. Avoid heavy pepper and earth, which overpower the whiskey's fruit. Example cigars: Ashton Classic – a smooth, creamy Connecticut shade cigar that pairs effortlessly with Jameson or Bushmills Original. t: Canadian Whisky and Rye: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: As a pairing group that started in Toronto, we have a soft spot for Canadian whisky. It's often dismissed as a mixer, but there are some excellent sipping whiskies coming out of…
x: As a pairing group that started in Toronto, we have a soft spot for Canadian whisky. It's often dismissed as a mixer, but there are some excellent sipping whiskies coming out of Canada, and American rye has gone from forgotten to fashionable in the last couple of decades. Both share a signature spice that opens up some great cigar pairings. Origin Canadian whisky began in the late 1700s and early 1800s with grist millers in Ontario and Quebec. They had surplus wheat and turned it into spirit. Many were German and Dutch immigrants who added a little rye to the mash for flavour. The spicy result became so popular that Canadians started calling all their whisky "rye," whether it contained much of the grain or not. The industry grew into some famous names: Gooderham & Worts in Toronto (1832), J.P. Wiser in Prescott (1857), and Hiram Walker, who founded his distillery across the river from Detroit in 1858 and created Canadian Club. American Prohibition (1920 to 1933) was a boom time. Canadian distilleries legally produced whisky that, one way or another, found its way across the border. American rye has its own history. It was the dominant whiskey of Pennsylvania and Maryland in the 1700s and 1800s, long before bourbon took over. After Prohibition it nearly vanished, but it has made a huge comeback with the cocktail revival. Where It's Traditionally Made Canadian whisky must be mashed, distilled and aged in Canada. Major producers are spread across Ontario (Hiram Walker, Canadian Mist), Quebec (Valleyfield), Manitoba (Gimli, home of Crown Royal) and Alberta (Alberta Distillers, Black Velvet). American rye can be made anywhere in the US. Today, many of the best-known ryes come from Kentucky and Indiana (Wild Turkey, Rittenhouse, Sazerac, Bulleit), with a growing craft scene in Pennsylvania and Maryland, rye's historic home. How It's Made Canadian whisky is usually made in a way that's quite different from Scotch or bourbon. Each grain (corn, wheat, rye, barley) is often fermented, distilled and aged separately , then blended at the end. A typical whisky combines a light, high-proof base spirit, usually corn, with a smaller amount of heavier, more flavourful rye whisky. By law, Canadian whisky must be aged at least three years in small wooden barrels (no larger than 700 litres) and bottled at 40% or more. It may contain caramel colouring and flavourings, and up to 9.09% of other spirits or wine can be blended in. There are exceptions to the blending norm: Alberta Premium, for example, is made from 100% rye. American rye follows the same rules as bourbon, but with rye in place of corn. The mash must contain at least 51% rye , and it must be aged in new, charred oak containers. "Straight rye" is aged at least two years. What It Tastes Like Most Canadian blends are light, smooth and sweet, with caramel, vanilla, a little dried fruit and a gentle rye spice on the finish. Whiskies with more rye (Alberta Premium, Lot No. 40, Crown Royal Northern Harvest) are spicier, with rye bread, pepper, clove and dark fruit. American rye is bolder and drier than bourbon, with black pepper, mint, dill, cinnamon and a lean, crisp finish. What to Look for in a Cigar Rye's defining feature is spice, so the main decision is whether to match that spice or balance it. Light Canadian blends: Go mild to medium so you don't drown the whisky. Connecticut and Ecuadorian shade wrappers with cream, nuts and sweetness work well. Try a Macanudo Cafe with Canadian Club or Crown Royal. High-rye Canadian and American rye: Match spice with spice. Nicaraguan and Habano-wrapped cigars bring black pepper, cedar and leather that line up with the rye. The Joya de Nicaragua Antaño 1970 is full, peppery and earthy, a bold match for a straight rye. The Oliva Serie V (Habano wrapper, spice and cocoa) is great with Lot No. 40 or Rittenhouse. t: Japanese Whisky: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: Japanese whisky has gone from a curiosity to one of the most sought-after spirits in the world in about twenty years. It owes a lot to Scotland, but it has developed its…
x: Japanese whisky has gone from a curiosity to one of the most sought-after spirits in the world in about twenty years. It owes a lot to Scotland, but it has developed its own personality: precise, balanced and often remarkably delicate. That subtlety makes it a rewarding, if slightly tricky, partner for a cigar. Origin The story of Japanese whisky begins with two men. Masataka Taketsuru, the son of a sake-brewing family, travelled to Scotland in 1918 to study chemistry at the University of Glasgow and apprentice at Scotch distilleries. He came home in 1920 with a notebook full of techniques and a Scottish wife, Rita. Shinjiro Torii, a businessman whose company would become Suntory, hired Taketsuru to build Japan's first commercial malt whisky distillery. It was built in Yamazaki, near Kyoto, in 1923, and the first Japanese whisky went on sale in 1929. Taketsuru later struck out on his own and in 1934 founded the Yoichi distillery on the northern island of Hokkaido. He chose the site because its cool, damp climate reminded him of Scotland. His company became Nikka. For decades, Japanese whisky was mostly drunk at home, often in highballs. Then a run of international awards in the 2000s turned it into a global sensation, and aged bottles became so scarce that many were discontinued. Where It's Traditionally Made The most famous distilleries are Suntory's Yamazaki (near Kyoto) and Hakushu (in the forested mountains of Yamanashi), and Nikka's Yoichi (Hokkaido) and Miyagikyo (near Sendai). Newer craft distilleries like Chichibu, Mars Shinshu and Akkeshi have earned cult followings. For years, Japan had almost no legal definition of whisky, and some bottles labelled "Japanese whisky" contained imported spirit. In 2021, the Japan Spirits & Liqueurs Makers Association adopted standards, fully in effect since 2024. To use the term, a whisky must be made from malted grain (other grains are allowed) using water from Japan. It must be fermented, distilled and aged in Japan, for at least three years in wooden casks, and bottled in Japan at 40% or more. How It's Made Production closely follows Scotch: malted barley, fermentation, distillation in copper pot stills (column stills for grain whisky), and oak aging. The big difference is how the industry is set up. Scottish blenders trade whisky freely between distilleries. Japanese companies traditionally don't, so each distillery learned to make many different styles in-house. They use a range of still shapes, yeasts, peating levels and cask types to build blends entirely from their own stock. Japanese distillers also use a rare native oak, mizunara . It's difficult to work with and prone to leaking, but it gives aged whisky a distinctive aroma of sandalwood, incense and coconut. Yoichi still heats some of its stills with coal fires, an old technique that adds weight and a slight smokiness. What It Tastes Like The house style is clean and balanced rather than bold. Expect honey, orchard fruit, citrus, vanilla and a light floral quality. Mizunara-aged whiskies add sandalwood and a gentle spice. Hakushu has a fresh, herbal, lightly smoky character. Yoichi can be robustly peaty and briny, closer to a coastal Scotch. What to Look for in a Cigar Treat most Japanese whisky the way you'd treat a fine Speyside or a lighter cognac. The goal is balance, not power. Strength: Mild to medium for blends like Hibiki or Toki and for lighter single malts like Yamazaki 12 or Hakushu. Medium to medium-full is fine for peated Yoichi or cask-strength releases. Wrapper: Connecticut shade and Ecuadorian wrappers suit the delicate, honeyed whiskies. Cuban-style cigars with cedar and a light spice are also excellent, which is why so many Japanese bars stock Cuban cigars. Flavours to look for: Cedar, cream, toasted almond, a touch of floral sweetness and gentle wood. Avoid heavy pepper and dark, earthy maduros with the lighter whiskies. They erase the subtle fruit and sandalwood that make the whisky special. Example ci

t: Cognac: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: Cognac and cigars are one of the great traditional pairings. Picture a leather armchair, a balloon glass and a long Cuban. There's a reason the image has lasted: a good cognac has…
x: Cognac and cigars are one of the great traditional pairings. Picture a leather armchair, a balloon glass and a long Cuban. There's a reason the image has lasted: a good cognac has the fruit, spice and silky texture to make a fine cigar taste even better. Here's how it's made and what to look for when you pick a smoke to go with it. Origin Cognac owes its existence to Dutch traders. In the 1500s and 1600s, Dutch ships sailed up the Charente river to buy salt and wine. The thin, acidic local wine didn't survive the sea voyage well, so traders began distilling it into brandewijn , "burnt wine," which kept far better and could be watered back down on arrival. That word became "brandy." Local producers soon discovered that distilling twice made a smoother spirit, and that the spirit improved dramatically when left in oak barrels. In the 1700s, the great cognac houses were founded: Martell in 1715, Rémy Martin in 1724, and Hennessy in 1765, started by Richard Hennessy, an Irish officer serving in the French army. The cognac region was officially defined in 1909, and the appellation was protected in 1936. Where It's Traditionally Made Cognac can only come from a defined area around the town of Cognac, in the Charente and Charente-Maritime departments of southwestern France. The region is divided into six growing areas, or crus , based on soil: Grande Champagne and Petite Champagne – chalky soils that produce the finest, longest-lived, most floral spirits. (The name comes from the chalky landscape, not the sparkling wine region.) Borderies – the smallest cru, known for nutty, violet-scented spirits. Fins Bois , Bons Bois and Bois Ordinaires – rounder, fruitier spirits that mature faster. "Fine Champagne" on a label means a blend of Grande and Petite Champagne, with at least half from Grande Champagne. How It's Made Cognac is made almost entirely from Ugni Blanc grapes, which produce a light, acidic, low-alcohol wine that's ideal for distilling. The wine is distilled twice in traditional copper Charentais alembic pot stills. The first distillation produces the brouillis at around 28 to 32% alcohol. The second, the bonne chauffe , produces a clear spirit of about 70%. By law, distillation must finish by March 31 following the harvest. The new spirit is then aged in French oak barrels, traditionally from the Limousin or Tronçais forests. Over the years it slowly loses alcohol and volume to evaporation, the famous "angels' share." Cellar masters blend spirits of different ages and crus to create each house style. The youngest spirit in the blend determines the age grade: VS (Very Special) – at least 2 years in oak VSOP (Very Superior Old Pale) – at least 4 years XO (Extra Old) – at least 10 years Many XO and "Hors d'Âge" blends contain spirits much older than the minimum. What It Tastes Like Young cognacs are fruity and lively, with fresh grape, pear, apricot, vanilla and a little spice. VSOPs add dried fruit, caramel, honey and toasted oak. Old XOs develop rancio , a prized savoury complexity with notes of walnut, mushroom, leather, candied orange, cigar box and old wood. What to Look for in a Cigar As we wrote in our brandy pairing guide , cognac is a strong drink that can handle a delicate cigar. It shouldn't be paired with something too dark or overpowering. You don't need to sacrifice flavour, you just need to choose the right one. Strength: Medium is the sweet spot. Mild cigars can work with a VS. Medium to medium-full suits VSOP and XO, especially older, rancio-heavy cognacs, which have more depth. Wrapper: Cameroon, Connecticut and Cuban wrappers are classic choices. They bring cedar, cream and gentle spice without burying the fruit. Be cautious with heavy maduros, which can turn a cognac flat and bitter. Flavours to look for: Cedar, milk chocolate, baking spice, toasted nuts, honey and floral notes. These complement cognac's fruit and oak and bring out the candied orange and vanilla. t: Armagnac: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: Armagnac is cognac's older, wilder cousin. It comes from a rural corner of Gascony and is mostly made by small family estates rather than big houses. It's bolder, more rustic and often…
x: Armagnac is cognac's older, wilder cousin. It comes from a rural corner of Gascony and is mostly made by small family estates rather than big houses. It's bolder, more rustic and often more complex than cognac, and it's one of our favourite spirits to pair with a cigar. You just need a cigar with enough backbone to keep up. Origin Armagnac is generally considered France's oldest brandy. A text written around 1310 by Vital Du Four, a prior in the Gascon town of Eauze, praises the "forty virtues" of the local aygue ardente (burning water). It claims the spirit could restore memory, cure gout and give courage. Distilling was a medicinal practice at first, but by the 1400s armagnac was being sold at local markets. Armagnac grew through trade with the Dutch, who bought it for shipping just as they did with cognac. But Gascony was further from major ports, so armagnac stayed a more local, artisanal product. The appellation was protected in 1936, and the region is still dominated by small producers, many of whom bottle single vintages. Where It's Traditionally Made Armagnac comes from Gascony in southwest France, mostly in the Gers department. The appellation has three areas: Bas-Armagnac – sandy soils that produce the finest, fruitiest and most elegant armagnacs. Most top estates are here. Armagnac-Ténarèze – clay and limestone soils that give fuller, more powerful spirits that need long aging. Haut-Armagnac – the largest area, but with very little production today. Well-known producers include Château de Laubade, Larressingle, Darroze, Delord and Château du Tariquet. How It's Made Ten grape varieties are allowed, but four dominate: Ugni Blanc, Baco Blanc (a hybrid grape almost unique to the region), Folle Blanche and Colombard. Baco brings a rich, round texture, while Folle Blanche gives floral elegance. The biggest difference from cognac is distillation. Most armagnac is distilled once in a traditional alambic armagnacais , a small copper column still. It comes off the still at a relatively low strength, usually around 52 to 60% alcohol. That keeps far more of the grape's flavour, aroma and oily texture than cognac's double distillation. The trade-off is a fiery young spirit that needs time in the barrel. Double distillation in pot stills is also permitted, and some houses use it. The spirit is aged in oak casks, traditionally local Gascon black oak, which is more tannic than the Limousin oak used for cognac. Age grades are similar to cognac's: VS – at least 1 year in oak VSOP – at least 4 years XO and Hors d'Âge – at least 10 years Armagnac is also famous for vintage bottlings, made from a single year's harvest. You can often find armagnac from your birth year at a reasonable price. Unaged "Blanche Armagnac" also exists, but it's rarely paired with cigars. What It Tastes Like Armagnac is bigger and earthier than cognac. Expect prunes, dried figs, raisins, toffee and dark caramel, with notes of leather, tobacco, licorice, walnut and spice. The finish is long and warming. Old Bas-Armagnacs can be incredibly complex, with an almost savoury rancio. Ténarèze bottlings tend to be more powerful and woody. What to Look for in a Cigar In our brandy pairing guide we said armagnac requires a more edgy cigar than cognac. That still holds. Strength: Medium-full to full. Armagnac's intensity and long finish will overwhelm a mild cigar. Wrapper: Habano, Sumatra and maduro wrappers all work. We'd generally avoid lighter Connecticut wrappers and delicate, grassy profiles. Many Cubans also feel a little too gentle here, though a fuller Cuban can still work. Flavours to look for: Earth, wood, leather, dark chocolate, coffee, a hint of spice and, if you can find it, dried fruit. These echo armagnac's prune and fig notes and stand up to its tannic grip. Example cigars: Rocky Patel Vintage 1992 – an aged Sumatra wrapper with cedar, cocoa and spice. A great everyday armagnac cigar. Alec Bradley Tempus – medium to full, with earth, wood and dark fruit.

t: Spanish Brandy: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: If cognac is elegant and armagnac is rustic, Spanish brandy is decadent. Brandy de Jerez is aged in old sherry casks using the solera system, and it's rich, sweet and dark, with…
x: If cognac is elegant and armagnac is rustic, Spanish brandy is decadent. Brandy de Jerez is aged in old sherry casks using the solera system, and it's rich, sweet and dark, with flavours of raisins, burnt caramel and nuts. It's one of the most generous cigar partners there is, and often one of the best values on the shelf. Origin Distillation arrived in Spain with the Moors, who ruled much of the Iberian Peninsula for nearly eight centuries. They used the alembic (from the Arabic al-anbiq ) to make perfumes and medicines. By the 1500s, Andalusian producers were distilling wine into strong spirits, called holandas because so much was sold to Dutch traders. It was also used to fortify sherry. A popular story says Brandy de Jerez was born by accident in the 1800s. A Dutch order for spirit was cancelled, and the barrels were left sitting in old sherry casks in a bodega. When someone finally tasted them, the spirit had turned into something wonderful. Whatever the truth, the first commercial brand to call itself brandy, Pedro Domecq's Fundador , was launched in Jerez in 1874. Where It's Traditionally Made Brandy de Jerez is a protected designation, and it must be aged in the "sherry triangle" formed by the towns of Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María in Andalusia. Interestingly, most of the base spirit is distilled elsewhere in Spain, largely from Airén grapes grown in La Mancha. It's the aging that must happen in Jerez. Spain's other major brandy region is Penedès in Catalonia, best known for Torres. Penedès brandies are often double distilled in pot stills and aged more like cognac, so they're a little lighter and drier than Brandy de Jerez. Well-known names include Cardenal Mendoza, Lepanto, Gran Duque d'Alba, Carlos I, Fundador and Torres. How It's Made Wine is distilled into holandas (low-strength spirit, under 70% alcohol, which keeps lots of grape character) or into higher-strength spirit. The spirit then goes into American oak casks that previously held sherry, often oloroso or Pedro Ximénez. These casks give the brandy its deep colour and much of its flavour. Aging uses the solera system. Barrels are stacked in tiers called criaderas . Brandy for bottling is drawn from the bottom tier (the solera ), which is then topped up from the tier above, and so on up the stack. The newest spirit goes in at the top. This constant blending means young brandy is "educated" by old brandy, and every bottle contains a small amount of very old spirit. Because of this, Brandy de Jerez is classified by average age: Solera – at least 6 months Solera Reserva – at least 1 year Solera Gran Reserva – at least 3 years (in practice, many top Gran Reservas average 10 to 15 years or more) In Spain, these brandies are often bottled at around 36% alcohol. Export versions for North America are usually bottled at 40% to meet import rules. What It Tastes Like Brandy de Jerez is rich, round and sweet-leaning, with raisins, dried figs, dates, burnt caramel, toffee, walnuts, cinnamon and chocolate. Oloroso casks bring nutty dryness, while Pedro Ximénez casks add sticky dark fruit and molasses. Penedès brandies are drier and more vanilla-oak driven. What to Look for in a Cigar As we put it in our brandy pairing guide , the flavours here are bold, dark and imposing, and the cigar needs to match. Strength: Medium-full to full. A mild cigar will be lost under the brandy's sweetness. Wrapper: Maduro and dark Habano wrappers are ideal. Their natural sugars and cocoa line up perfectly with the sherry-cask fruit. Flavours to look for: Wet earth, dark chocolate, espresso, leather and dark dried fruit. If the brandy is very sweet, a spicier cigar keeps the pair from becoming syrupy. Example cigars: Arturo Fuente Añejo – a Connecticut broadleaf maduro made with tobacco aged in cognac barrels. It's rich, sweet and spicy, a superb match for a Solera Gran Reserva. La Aurora 100 Años – medium-full and earthy, with leather and spice. Ram

t: Calvados: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: In our original brandy guide we admitted to keeping a decanter of Calvados on the desk "in case I need a quick but reliable pairing drink." It's still true. Calvados, the apple…
x: In our original brandy guide we admitted to keeping a decanter of Calvados on the desk "in case I need a quick but reliable pairing drink." It's still true. Calvados, the apple brandy of Normandy, is warm, fruity and spicy without being heavy. It's one of the most versatile cigar partners around, and still something of a hidden gem. Origin Normandy is too cool and damp for wine grapes, but perfect for apples, and cider has been made there for well over a thousand years. The first recorded distillation of cider in Normandy comes from 1553, in the diary of a nobleman named Gilles de Gouberville. Distillers formed a guild in the early 1600s, and apple brandy became the region's signature spirit. The name comes from the Calvados department, created in 1790. Local legend says the department itself was named after El Calvador , a ship from the Spanish Armada wrecked off the Normandy coast in 1588. Calvados gained legal protection in 1942, and its three appellations have been refined since. Where It's Traditionally Made Calvados can only be made in parts of Normandy (and a few neighbouring areas). There are three appellations: AOC Calvados – the largest area. It's usually distilled once in a column still and aged at least 2 years. Fresh and fruity. Calvados Pays d'Auge – the most prestigious, from the heart of Normandy's orchard country. It must be double distilled in copper pot stills and aged at least 2 years, which makes it richer and more complex. Calvados Domfrontais – must contain at least 30% perry pears, is column distilled and aged at least 3 years. Elegant, floral and pear-driven. Well-known producers include Christian Drouin, Boulard, Père Magloire, Roger Groult, Pierre Huet and Lecompte. How It's Made Calvados starts in the orchard. Producers use special cider apples rather than eating apples. There are hundreds of varieties, grouped as sweet, bittersweet, bitter and sharp, and blended for balance. Pears are used too, especially in Domfrontais. In traditional orchards, cows graze between tall, old trees. The fruit is crushed and pressed, and the juice is slowly fermented into dry cider for at least a month (six weeks in Pays d'Auge). The cider is then distilled into clear eau-de-vie and aged in oak casks, often large old barrels that let the fruit shine. Age statements work much like cognac's, based on the youngest spirit in the blend: Fine or VS – at least 2 years Vieux or Réserve – at least 3 years VO , VSOP or Vieille Réserve – at least 4 years XO , Hors d'Âge or Très Vieille Réserve – at least 6 years Vintage calvados and very old age statements (15, 20, 30 years) are also available. What It Tastes Like Young calvados is bright and crisp: fresh apple, pear, apple blossom and a little spice. With age it moves toward baked apple, tarte tatin, cinnamon, vanilla, toffee and toasted nuts. The oldest calvados take on notes of leather, dried apple, honey and old oak. Pays d'Auge bottlings are typically rounder and more complex, while Domfrontais is lighter and more floral. What to Look for in a Cigar Calvados's strength is its fruit, so the cigar should support that fruit rather than bury it. Strength: Mild to medium for young calvados. Medium, or occasionally medium-full, for older XO and Hors d'Âge bottlings. Wrapper: Connecticut shade and Cameroon wrappers are excellent with young calvados. Their creaminess and gentle sweetness are like cream poured over apple pie. For older calvados, a medium Habano or Cameroon wrapper with more spice works well. Flavours to look for: Cream, cedar, baking spice (especially cinnamon and nutmeg), toasted nuts and honey. These complement the apple. For contrast, a little pepper can liven up a very soft, sweet calvados. Example cigars: Oliva Connecticut Reserve – smooth and creamy with a touch of nuttiness. A natural match for a young AOC Calvados or a Fine Pays d'Auge. Romeo y Julieta Reserva Real – a mild to medium Ecuadorian Connecticut, with cedar and light spice. Lovely with a VSOP. Ar

t: Rum: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: Rum and cigars grow up in the same neighbourhood. Sugar cane and tobacco thrive in the same tropical climates, and many of the best rums come from countries that also make world-class…
x: Rum and cigars grow up in the same neighbourhood. Sugar cane and tobacco thrive in the same tropical climates, and many of the best rums come from countries that also make world-class cigars: Cuba, the Dominican Republic and Nicaragua. It's no surprise that a good aged rum is one of the most natural cigar pairings there is. Origin Christopher Columbus brought sugar cane to the Caribbean on his second voyage in 1493, and sugar plantations spread across the islands. Making sugar leaves behind huge amounts of a sticky by-product called molasses. In the 1600s, on the plantations of Barbados, someone discovered that molasses could be fermented and distilled. A 1651 account describes the result, "Rumbullion, alias Kill-Divill," as "a hot, hellish, and terrible liquor." The name was shortened to rum. Rum's history is inseparable from the colonial sugar trade and the enslavement of millions of Africans who worked the plantations. It's an uncomfortable story, but an important one to acknowledge. Rum also became the drink of the Royal Navy, which issued sailors a daily ration from 1655 until "Black Tot Day" on July 31, 1970. Mount Gay in Barbados, with records dating back to 1703, is widely regarded as the oldest rum brand still operating. Where It's Traditionally Made Rum is made all over the world, but its heartland is the Caribbean and Latin America. Different colonial histories produced three broad styles: Spanish style (Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic, Venezuela, Panama, Nicaragua, Guatemala) – lighter, smoother rums, mostly from column stills. Think Havana Club, Brugal, Diplomático, Flor de Caña and Ron Zacapa. English style (Jamaica, Barbados, Guyana) – heavier, more flavourful rums, often from pot stills. Jamaican rum is famous for its "funky" tropical fruit character. Appleton Estate, Mount Gay and El Dorado are classics. French style (Martinique, Guadeloupe) – rhum agricole , made from fresh sugar cane juice rather than molasses. Martinique's rhum agricole has had its own protected appellation since 1996. Rhum J.M, Clément and Neisson are well-known producers. How It's Made Most rum starts with molasses , which is diluted with water and fermented. Fermentation can take a day or two for light rums, or several weeks for heavy Jamaican styles, which develop intense fruity esters. Rhum agricole is made from freshly pressed cane juice , which gives it a grassy, vegetal character. The fermented "wash" is distilled in column stills (lighter, cleaner rum), pot stills (heavier, more flavourful rum), or both, then blended. Aged rums are usually matured in ex-bourbon barrels. In the tropical heat, rum ages much faster than whisky does in Scotland, and much more is lost to evaporation each year. Unlike Scotch or cognac, rum has no single set of global rules. Each country sets its own standards, and some have very few. Watch out for numbers on labels: a "23" on a solera rum like Ron Zacapa doesn't mean every drop is 23 years old. Some rums also contain added sugar, which can make them taste sweeter and heavier than the age suggests. What It Tastes Like Light Spanish-style rums are clean and gently sweet, with vanilla and a little fruit. Aged Spanish-style rums add caramel, toffee, cocoa, coffee and dried fruit. English-style rums are bolder, with banana, pineapple, molasses, baking spice and sometimes a funky, overripe fruit note. Rhum agricole is grassy, peppery and floral when young, and develops into something cognac-like with age. What to Look for in a Cigar Rum may be the easiest spirit to pair with a cigar, but the best pairings still follow the same rules: balance the strength and look for shared flavours. Strength: Medium to full for aged sipping rums. Many are bottled at 40%, and their sweetness can take a robust cigar. Lighter rums need a mild to medium cigar. Wrapper: Maduro wrappers are a classic match for dark, aged rums. Their sweetness, cocoa and coffee mirror the molasses and caramel. Habano and Dominican wrapper

t: Tequila: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: Most people's first tequila memory involves salt, lime and regret. Good tequila is a different animal entirely. A well-made añejo can be as complex as a fine whisky, and even a crisp…
x: Most people's first tequila memory involves salt, lime and regret. Good tequila is a different animal entirely. A well-made añejo can be as complex as a fine whisky, and even a crisp blanco can make a surprisingly refreshing cigar partner. Here's how tequila is made and how to match each style with the right smoke. Origin Long before tequila, the Aztecs and other peoples of Mexico fermented the sap of the agave plant into pulque , a milky, mildly alcoholic drink with religious significance. When the Spanish arrived in the 1500s, they brought distillation. They began distilling agave into what they called "mezcal wine." The area around the town of Tequila, in the state of Jalisco, became famous for its agave spirit. In 1758, José Antonio de Cuervo received a land grant there to grow agave, and in 1795 his son received the first official licence to produce it commercially. In 1873, Don Cenobio Sauza became the first to export tequila to the United States, and he helped establish blue agave as the best variety. Mexico declared tequila a protected designation of origin in 1974. Where It's Traditionally Made Tequila can only be made in Mexico, in the state of Jalisco and in certain municipalities of Guanajuato, Michoacán, Nayarit and Tamaulipas. Within Jalisco there are two main growing areas: The Highlands (Los Altos) – red, iron-rich soil and cooler temperatures produce larger, sweeter agave. Highland tequilas tend to be fruity, floral and soft. The Lowlands (Tequila Valley) – volcanic soil gives earthier, more herbal and peppery tequilas. How It's Made All tequila must be made from blue Weber agave ( Agave tequilana ). Agave is not a cactus. It's a succulent that takes roughly six to eight years to mature. When it's ready, skilled harvesters called jimadores cut away the long, spiky leaves to reveal the heart, or piña , which can weigh 40 kilograms or more. The piñas are cooked to turn their starches into fermentable sugars. Traditionally this was done slowly in brick ovens ( hornos ). Many producers now use faster steel autoclaves, and some use industrial diffusers, which many purists feel strip out flavour. The cooked agave is crushed to extract the juice. A few traditional producers still use a tahona , a huge volcanic stone wheel. The juice is fermented and then distilled at least twice. Look for "100% agave" on the label. Tequila without it is a "mixto," which only needs to contain 51% agave sugars. The rest can come from other sugars. Tequila is then classified by aging: Blanco (or Plata) – unaged, or rested for less than two months Reposado ("rested") – aged 2 months to under a year in oak Añejo ("aged") – 1 to 3 years in oak barrels of no more than 600 litres Extra Añejo – at least 3 years in oak Ex-bourbon barrels are the most common, though some producers use wine, sherry or cognac casks. What It Tastes Like Blanco is the purest expression of the agave: cooked agave, citrus, black pepper, green herbs and sometimes a mineral, briny note. Reposado keeps that agave character and adds vanilla, caramel and a soft oakiness. Añejo and extra añejo become rich and smooth, with butterscotch, toasted oak, dried fruit, chocolate and baking spice, sometimes drinking more like a fine bourbon or cognac. What to Look for in a Cigar With tequila, the age statement tells you almost everything you need to know about your cigar choice. Blanco: Keep the cigar mild to medium so the agave can shine. Connecticut and Ecuadorian wrappers with cream, citrus and light pepper complement blanco's brightness. Heavy maduros tend to clash with the vegetal agave. Try a Perdomo Reserve 10th Anniversary Champagne . Reposado: Step up to medium. Habano and Sumatra wrappers with cedar, light spice and a little sweetness pick up the vanilla and oak while respecting the agave. A Rocky Patel Decade is a good match. Añejo and Extra Añejo: Treat these like a bourbon. Medium-full cigars with cocoa, coffee, caramel and leather all work, and maduros are now fair g

t: Mezcal: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: If tequila is agave in its cleanest form, mezcal is agave with the campfire still burning. Its smoky, earthy, wild character has won a devoted following, and for cigar smokers it's an…
x: If tequila is agave in its cleanest form, mezcal is agave with the campfire still burning. Its smoky, earthy, wild character has won a devoted following, and for cigar smokers it's an intriguing pairing. Think of it as the Islay Scotch of the agave world: smoke meeting smoke. Origin The word mezcal comes from the Nahuatl mexcalli , meaning "cooked agave." People in Mexico have roasted and eaten agave for thousands of years, and fermented its sap into pulque long before the Spanish arrived. Most historians believe agave was first distilled after Spanish contact in the 1500s. One theory suggests Filipino sailors on the Manila galleons introduced simple stills to Mexico's Pacific coast. Others argue for older, pre-Hispanic distillation. The debate is still lively. Technically, tequila is a type of mezcal, the one from Jalisco made with blue agave, that went its own way. Mezcal remained a rural, village spirit made in small batches for local celebrations. It received its own designation of origin in 1994. Over the last two decades it has gone from a regional curiosity to a cocktail-bar staple. Where It's Traditionally Made The mezcal designation of origin covers several Mexican states, including Oaxaca, Durango, Guerrero, San Luis Potosí, Zacatecas, and parts of Guanajuato, Tamaulipas, Michoacán and Puebla. Oaxaca is the undisputed heart of mezcal and produces the vast majority of it, especially around Santiago Matatlán, known as the "world capital of mezcal." Mezcal is still mostly made by family producers, called mezcaleros , at small rustic distilleries known as palenques . Recipes and techniques are often handed down through generations. How It's Made Unlike tequila, mezcal can be made from many species of agave. Espadín is by far the most common because it matures relatively quickly, in around six to eight years. Wild and semi-wild agaves like tobalá , tepeztate and madrecuixe can take 12 to 25 years or more to mature. They produce smaller, pricier and often extraordinary batches. The defining step is the roast. The agave hearts ( piñas ) are cooked in a conical pit dug into the ground, lined with wood and volcanic stones heated until they glow. The piñas are piled on top, covered with agave fibres and earth, and left to roast for several days. This is where mezcal's signature smoke comes from. The roasted agave is crushed, traditionally by a tahona stone wheel pulled by a horse or donkey, or even pounded by hand with wooden mallets. It's then fermented naturally with wild yeasts in open wooden vats, sometimes in vats made of stone or animal hide. Finally it's distilled, usually twice, in small copper or clay pot stills. Mexican rules define three categories based on method: Mezcal – modern equipment allowed Mezcal Artesanal – pit-roasted, traditional crushing and fermentation, copper or clay pot stills Mezcal Ancestral – the most traditional of all: pit-roasted, hand-pounded or tahona-crushed, and distilled in clay pots over direct fire Most mezcal is bottled unaged ( joven or blanco ), because producers want the agave to speak. Reposado and añejo versions do exist. What It Tastes Like Smoke is the headline, but good mezcal is far more than smoke. Espadín typically shows roasted agave, smoke, citrus, tropical fruit and black pepper. Tobalá can be floral and sweet, tepeztate intensely herbal and spicy, and other wild agaves earthy, mineral or even a little funky. Mezcals are often bottled at 45% to 50% alcohol or more, so they're powerful. What to Look for in a Cigar As with peated Scotch, you can either match mezcal's smoke or balance it. Strength: Medium-full to full. Mezcal's proof, smoke and intensity will flatten a mild cigar. Wrapper: Maduro wrappers, especially Mexican San Andrés and Connecticut broadleaf, are excellent. Their natural sweetness and cocoa soften the smoke and bring out the roasted agave's sweetness. Mexican San Andrés tobacco adds a nice element of shared heritage too. Flavours to look for: Dark chocol

t: Port: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: Port was one of the very first drinks we paired on this site. Our early reviews matched Taylor Fladgate tawny with a Partagás, and a 1983 Warre's vintage with a Cohiba. It's…
x: Port was one of the very first drinks we paired on this site. Our early reviews matched Taylor Fladgate tawny with a Partagás, and a 1983 Warre's vintage with a Cohiba. It's still one of the most satisfying after-dinner pairings you can make. Port is sweet, rich and lower in alcohol than spirits, so it plays beautifully with a full-flavoured cigar. Origin Port's story is as much English as Portuguese. In the late 1600s, England was frequently at war with France and looked to Portugal for wine instead. The Methuen Treaty of 1703 cut tariffs on Portuguese wines, and British merchants flooded into the city of Porto. To help the red wines of the Douro Valley survive the voyage to England, shippers added brandy. They eventually discovered that adding it during fermentation produced a richer, sweeter and more stable wine. In 1756, the Marquis of Pombal officially demarcated the Douro Valley to protect port's quality. It was one of the first demarcated wine regions in the world. Many of the great port houses still carry British names: Taylor's (founded 1692), Warre's (1670), Croft, Graham's, Dow's, Cockburn's and Sandeman. Where It's Traditionally Made Port's grapes are grown in the Douro Valley in northern Portugal, on dramatic terraced slopes of schist above the Douro river. The summers are scorching and the vineyards are some of the most beautiful (and hardest to work) in the world. The valley has three sub-regions: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo, and the remote Douro Superior. Traditionally, the young wine was shipped downriver in flat-bottomed boats called rabelos to the port lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across the river from Porto, where it was aged and bottled. Many houses still age their wines there. How It's Made More than 80 grape varieties are permitted, but five are considered the best: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão. Many top ports are still made by crushing grapes underfoot in shallow stone tanks called lagares , a gentle method that extracts colour and tannin quickly. The key step is fortification . After only two or three days of fermentation, while the wine is still sweet, it's run off and mixed with a clear grape spirit called aguardente (about 77% alcohol), roughly one part spirit to four parts wine. The spirit kills the yeast and stops fermentation, leaving natural grape sugar in the wine and raising the alcohol to around 19 to 22%. What happens next determines the style: Ruby – aged briefly in large vats to keep its bright, fruity character. "Reserve" rubies are a step up. Late Bottled Vintage (LBV) – wine from a single year, aged 4 to 6 years in wood before bottling. A great-value taste of vintage style. Vintage – made only in the best years, when a house "declares" a vintage. It spends about two years in wood, then ages for decades in the bottle. It throws a sediment and needs decanting. Tawny – aged in small casks, where slow oxidation turns it amber-brown and nutty. 10, 20, 30 and 40 year tawnies are labelled by an approximate average age. Colheita – a single-vintage tawny aged at least 7 years in wood. White and Rosé – lighter styles, usually served chilled or in cocktails. What It Tastes Like Ruby, LBV and vintage ports are deep purple and full of dark fruit: blackberry, plum, cassis and cherry, with chocolate, violet and spice. Old vintage ports soften into dried fruit, leather and cedar. Tawny ports are a completely different experience: caramel, toffee, walnut, almond, dried fig, orange peel and butterscotch, getting more concentrated with age. What to Look for in a Cigar Port's sweetness and lower alcohol give you a lot of freedom. The rule of thumb: match ruby and vintage ports with rich, dark cigars, and tawnies with nutty, medium-bodied ones. Ruby, LBV and vintage: Go medium-full to full. Maduro and dark Habano wrappers bring cocoa, espresso and earth that turn the port's dark fruit into something like chocolate-covered cherries. Try a Padrón 1926 S

t: Sherry: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: Sherry gives Scotch, Spanish brandy and even some rums much of their character, through the casks it leaves behind. Yet the wine itself is often overlooked. That's a shame, because sherry is…
x: Sherry gives Scotch, Spanish brandy and even some rums much of their character, through the casks it leaves behind. Yet the wine itself is often overlooked. That's a shame, because sherry is one of the world's great wines and a brilliant, very varied cigar partner. A good amontillado or oloroso with a cigar is a revelation. Origin Wine has been made around Jerez for about 3,000 years, since Phoenician traders planted vines near Cádiz. Under Moorish rule (from 711 to 1492) the town was called Sherish , which eventually gave us the word "sherry." Distillation also arrived with the Moors, and in time the local spirit was used to fortify the wines. The English fell in love with sherry, which they called "sack." Shakespeare's Falstaff praises it at length. In 1587, Sir Francis Drake raided Cádiz and carried off around 2,900 barrels of it, which did wonders for its popularity in London. British and Irish merchants later founded or partnered in many of the great bodegas, which is why names like Harveys, Osborne and Garvey appear alongside Spanish ones like González Byass, Lustau and Hidalgo. Sherry became Spain's first protected designation of origin in 1933. Where It's Traditionally Made Sherry comes from the "sherry triangle" in Andalusia, in southwest Spain, formed by three towns: Jerez de la Frontera , Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María . Sherry must be aged in one of these towns. The best vineyards grow on albariza , a brilliant white chalky soil that holds moisture through the hot, dry summers. Cooling Atlantic breezes help, especially in the seaside town of Sanlúcar. How It's Made Most sherry is made from the Palomino grape, which makes a neutral, dry base wine. Sweet sherries are made from Pedro Ximénez (PX) or Moscatel grapes, which are often sun-dried into raisins before pressing. After fermentation, the wine is fortified with grape spirit, and the winemaker decides which path it will take: Biological aging: wines fortified to about 15% grow a layer of yeast called flor on their surface. The flor protects the wine from oxygen and gives it a tangy, bready, saline character. This makes Fino and, in Sanlúcar, Manzanilla . Oxidative aging: wines fortified to about 17% or more can't support flor, so they age in contact with air, darkening and gaining nutty richness. This makes Oloroso . Both: Amontillado starts life under flor, then the flor dies off and the wine continues aging oxidatively. Palo Cortado is a rare, prized style that combines amontillado's elegance with oloroso's richness. All sherry ages in the solera system. Barrels are arranged in tiers. Wine for bottling is drawn from the oldest tier, which is topped up from the next-oldest, and so on, with new wine going in at the top. Every bottle is a blend of many vintages, with a minimum average age of two years. Labels marked VOS (20+ years average) and VORS (30+ years) indicate very old sherries. Sweet PX and Moscatel sherries, and blended "cream" sherries, round out the range. What It Tastes Like Fino and Manzanilla – pale, bone-dry and crisp: almonds, bread dough, green apple and sea salt. Amontillado – amber and dry: hazelnut, toffee, dried orange peel and a savoury tang. Oloroso – mahogany and dry (despite its rich aroma): walnut, leather, tobacco, dried fruit and spice. Pedro Ximénez – almost black and very sweet: raisins, figs, molasses, coffee and chocolate. What to Look for in a Cigar There's a sherry for almost any cigar. The style determines everything, so match the cigar's weight to the wine's. Fino and Manzanilla: These are delicate, chilled and lower in alcohol. Choose a mild Connecticut shade cigar with cream and nuts, and keep it short. A Romeo y Julieta Reserva Real works nicely. Anything bolder will overwhelm the wine. Amontillado and Oloroso: This is where sherry really shines with cigars. Go medium to medium-full. Cuban, Habano and Cameroon wrappers bring cedar, leather, toasted nuts and spice that echo the wine's nutty dryness. The

t: Gin: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: Gin isn't the first spirit most people think of for a cigar, but it deserves a closer look. A crisp London Dry, a softly sweet Old Tom or a malty Dutch genever…
x: Gin isn't the first spirit most people think of for a cigar, but it deserves a closer look. A crisp London Dry, a softly sweet Old Tom or a malty Dutch genever can each make an interesting pairing. On a hot summer afternoon, a well-made gin and tonic with a light cigar is hard to beat. You just need to choose your cigar with care. Origin Gin's ancestor is genever (or jenever ), a malty, juniper-flavoured spirit from the Low Countries. Juniper had been used as medicine for centuries, and by the 1500s and 1600s Dutch and Flemish distillers were making genever in quantity. English soldiers fighting alongside the Dutch in the Thirty Years' War are said to have taken a swig before battle, giving us the phrase "Dutch courage." When the Dutch prince William of Orange took the English throne in 1689, gin came with him. The government encouraged local distilling and taxed French brandy heavily, and London went gin-mad. During the "Gin Craze" of the early 1700s, cheap, rough gin was blamed for widespread social problems, captured in William Hogarth's famous print Gin Lane (1751). A series of Gin Acts eventually brought it under control. The arrival of the column still in the 1830s made it possible to produce a clean, neutral spirit. That gave rise to the crisp, unsweetened London Dry style. Meanwhile, the British in India mixed their bitter quinine tonic with gin to make it palatable, and the gin and tonic was born. Where It's Traditionally Made Gin is now made everywhere, but its traditional homes are: The Netherlands and Belgium – genever, which has its own protected status. England – especially London, home of Beefeater, Sipsmith and many others. Despite the name, "London Dry" describes a method, not a place, and can be made anywhere. Tanqueray and Bombay Sapphire are distilled outside London. Plymouth – Plymouth Gin, an earthier, softer style, has been distilled in the city since 1793. Since the 2000s, a craft gin boom has produced thousands of new gins worldwide, many using local botanicals. How It's Made Most gin starts with a neutral spirit, usually made from grain. It's then flavoured with botanicals , and juniper must be the predominant flavour. Other common botanicals include coriander seed, angelica root, orris root, citrus peel, cassia, cardamom and licorice. There are two main ways to add the botanicals during redistillation: Steeping – the botanicals soak in the spirit, sometimes overnight, and then everything is distilled together. Vapour infusion – the botanicals sit in a basket above the spirit, and the rising vapour picks up their aromas. This gives a lighter, more delicate result (Bombay Sapphire is the famous example). London Dry gin must get all of its flavour from botanicals during distillation, with nothing added afterward except water and a tiny amount of sugar. Other styles include Old Tom (lightly sweetened, popular in the 1800s), Plymouth , New Western or contemporary gins (where juniper takes a back seat to other botanicals), and barrel-aged gins. Genever is made differently, from a base of malt wine (a pot-distilled spirit from malted grain), which gives it a whisky-like body. What It Tastes Like London Dry gin is crisp and dry: pine-like juniper, citrus, coriander spice and earthy roots. Old Tom is rounder and sweeter. Contemporary gins can lean floral, herbal, citrusy or spicy, depending on their botanicals. Barrel-aged gins add vanilla and soft oak. Genever is malty and bready, somewhere between gin and a light whisky. What to Look for in a Cigar Gin's aromatic botanicals are easy to overwhelm, so the cigar should be light enough to let them through. Strength: Mild to medium. A full-bodied maduro will flatten a London Dry completely. Wrapper: Connecticut shade and Cameroon wrappers are ideal. Their cream, cedar and light floral notes complement the juniper and citrus. Flavours to look for: Cedar, cream, white pepper, citrus, floral and herbal notes. Cedar and juniper are a particularly nice match, since

t: Vodka: Origin, Production, and Cigar Pairing
s: Let's be honest up front: vodka is not a classic cigar pairing. Our whole approach to pairing is that the drink and the cigar should each make the other better, and most…
x: Let's be honest up front: vodka is not a classic cigar pairing. Our whole approach to pairing is that the drink and the cigar should each make the other better, and most vodka is designed to taste of very little. But that doesn't mean it's useless with a cigar. Good vodka has more character than people think, and used the right way, it can be a clean, refreshing companion to a mild smoke. Origin Poland and Russia have argued for centuries over who invented vodka. The name in both languages is a diminutive of "water" ( woda in Polish, voda in Russian), so it means something like "little water." Polish court records from Sandomierz mention wódka in 1405, though probably as a medicine. Russian tradition credits monks in Moscow with distilling grain spirit in the 1400s. Like most of these stories, the details are hard to prove. Early vodka was often harsh and flavoured with herbs, honey or fruit to make it palatable. Over time, distillers learned to make purer spirits through repeated distillation and charcoal filtering. Vodka became central to life in Russia, where the state held a vodka monopoly at various times. It only took off in the West after the Second World War, eventually becoming one of the best-selling spirits in the world. Where It's Traditionally Made Vodka's traditional home is the "vodka belt" of Eastern and Northern Europe: Poland , Russia , Ukraine , Belarus , the Baltic states and Scandinavia . Sweden gives us Absolut, Finland gives us Finlandia, and Poland is known for Belvedere, Chopin and Żubrówka (bison grass vodka). "Polish Vodka" is a protected designation that must be made in Poland from Polish rye, wheat, barley, oats, triticale or potatoes. Today vodka is made all over the world, including popular brands from France (Grey Goose), the Netherlands (Ketel One) and the United States (Tito's). How It's Made Vodka can be made from almost anything that ferments. Grains (wheat, rye, corn, barley) and potatoes are traditional, but grapes, sugar beet and even milk whey are also used. The raw material is fermented and then distilled to a very high strength, typically around 95 to 96% alcohol, usually in column stills. At that strength, most of the flavour from the raw material is stripped away. Many vodkas are then filtered, often through charcoal, to remove remaining impurities and smooth the texture. The spirit is diluted with water to bottling strength: at least 37.5% in the European Union and 40% in the United States. Vodka is not aged. Interestingly, the US used to define vodka as having "no distinctive character, aroma, taste or colour." That wording was dropped in 2020, recognising that good vodka does have character. What It Tastes Like Vodka is subtle, but the base ingredient still shows through in better bottles: Rye vodka – spicy, peppery and bready, with a firm finish (Belvedere, Sobieski). Wheat vodka – soft, light and slightly sweet, sometimes with a hint of anise (Grey Goose, Ketel One). Potato vodka – creamy, full-bodied and earthy (Chopin Potato). Corn vodka – round and gently sweet (Tito's). Texture matters a lot with vodka. Served ice cold, a good vodka becomes thick and almost syrupy. What to Look for in a Cigar Since vodka brings little flavour of its own, think of it as a palate cleanser rather than a flavour partner. Its job is to refresh your mouth between puffs, so you taste the cigar more clearly. Strength: Mild to medium. A strong cigar won't interact with the vodka at all. It will simply dominate it, and the alcohol can make a full-bodied cigar feel harsh. Wrapper: Connecticut shade wrappers are the natural choice. Their cream, light cedar and gentle sweetness complement the soft, clean texture of a chilled wheat or potato vodka. Flavours to look for: Cream, butter, light nuttiness, cedar and a touch of sweetness. With a peppery rye vodka, a cigar with a little white pepper can make a nice echo.
